title: MATH2010 Module 09: Coordinate Systems & Linear Transformations

questions.q: Let B = {b₁, ..., bₙ} be a basis for a vector space V. What does the Unique Representation Theorem guarantee for each x in V?
choices: There is exactly one set of scalars c₁, ..., cₙ with x = c₁b₁ + ... + cₙbₙ.
There are infinitely many sets of scalars c₁, ..., cₙ with x = c₁b₁ + ... + cₙbₙ.
There is at least one set of scalars with x = c₁b₁ + ... + cₙbₙ, but there may be several.
x is equal to one of the basis vectors bᵢ.
questions.explain: A basis spans V, so at least one representation exists. A basis is linearly independent, so there is at most one. Together this gives exactly one.

questions.q: In the uniqueness proof, two representations x = Σ cᵢbᵢ and x = Σ dᵢbᵢ are subtracted to get 0 = Σ (cᵢ - dᵢ)bᵢ. Which property of the basis then forces cᵢ = dᵢ for every i?
choices: The basis vectors are linearly independent.
The basis vectors span V.
The basis contains the standard basis vectors.
The basis contains the zero vector.
questions.explain: Linear independence means the only combination of the bᵢ equal to 0 is the trivial one, so every cᵢ - dᵢ = 0. Spanning only guarantees that a representation exists.

questions.q: If {v₁, ..., vₚ} spans V but is linearly dependent, then every x in V can be written in infinitely many ways as a linear combination of v₁, ..., vₚ.
questions.explain: Spanning gives at least one representation. Adding any multiple of a nontrivial dependence relation (a combination equal to 0) gives another one, so there are infinitely many.

questions.q: If a set of vectors in ℝ³ is not a basis for ℝ³, then every x in ℝ³ can be written in infinitely many ways as a linear combination of those vectors.
questions.explain: If x is not in the span of the set, there are zero representations. If the set is independent but does not span, each x in the span has exactly one. Infinitely many representations happen only when x is in the span and the set is dependent.

questions.q: Let v₁ = (1, 1, 3), v₂ = (2, 1, 1), v₃ = (3, 2, 4), and x = (1, 0, -2). Which of these are valid ways to write x?
choices: x = -v₁ + v₂
x = -2v₁ + v₃
x = 2v₂ - v₃
x = v₁ - v₂
x = -3v₁ - v₂ + 2v₃
x = -v₁ + v₂ + v₃
questions.explain: Row reducing gives (c₁, c₂, c₃) = (-1 - t, 1 - t, t). t = 0, 1, -1, 2 give the four correct choices. v₁ - v₂ = (-1, 0, 2), which is -x. -v₁ + v₂ + v₃ = x + v₃ = (4, 2, 2).

questions.q: For v₁ = (1, 1, 3), v₂ = (2, 1, 1), v₃ = (3, 2, 4), and x = (1, 0, -2), the solutions of c₁v₁ + c₂v₂ + c₃v₃ = x are (c₁, c₂, c₃) = (-1, 1, 0) + t(-1, -1, 1). What does the direction vector (-1, -1, 1) represent?
choices: The weights of the dependence relation -v₁ - v₂ + v₃ = 0.
The coordinate vector of x relative to {v₁, v₂, v₃}.
A sign that x is not in the span of v₁, v₂, v₃.
A second vector that x must equal.
questions.explain: v₃ = v₁ + v₂, so -v₁ - v₂ + v₃ = 0. Adding any multiple of this relation to one representation of x gives another. That is exactly how uniqueness fails without linear independence.

questions.q: Let B = {b₁, b₂, b₃, b₄} be a basis for V. What is [b₃]_B?
choices: b₃ itself
questions.explain: b₃ = 0b₁ + 0b₂ + 1b₃ + 0b₄, so its B-coordinates are (0, 0, 1, 0) = e₃.

questions.q: With B = {(1, -1, 3), (2, -3, 1), (5, -1, 2)}, the coordinate vector [x]_B = (2, -3, 1) happens to equal the second basis vector. This means x = (2, -3, 1).
questions.explain: x and [x]_B are different objects. Here x = (1, 6, 5). For x to equal b₂, you would need [x]_B = e₂ = (0, 1, 0).

questions.q: Let B = {(1, 2), (-1, 1)}, a basis for ℝ². If [x]_B = (3, 2), what is x?
Let B = {(1, 2), (-1, 1)}, a basis for ℝ². If x = (0, 6), what is [x]_B?
questions.explain: Solve c₁(1, 2) + c₂(-1, 1) = (0, 6): c₁ - c₂ = 0 and 2c₁ + c₂ = 6, so c₁ = c₂ = 2. Check: 2(1, 2) + 2(-1, 1) = (0, 6). (-6, 6) is what you get by multiplying x by the basis matrix, which goes the wrong direction.

questions.q: The coordinate vector [x]_B does not depend on the order in which the basis vectors of B are listed.
questions.explain: A basis used for coordinates is ordered. Swapping b₁ and b₂ swaps the first two entries of [x]_B.

questions.q: Let B be a basis of V with n vectors. Which statements about the coordinate mapping C : V → ℝⁿ, C(x) = [x]_B, are true?
choices: C is a linear transformation.
C is one-to-one.
C maps V onto ℝⁿ.
C is only defined when V is ℝⁿ.
C sends every basis vector bᵢ to the zero vector.
questions.explain: The theorem says C is a one-to-one linear transformation from V onto ℝⁿ. V can be any vector space with a basis of n vectors, such as ℙₙ₋₁. C sends bᵢ to eᵢ, not to 0.

questions.q: Relative to a basis B, [u]_B = (1, -2, 0) and [w]_B = (3, 1, 4). What is [2u - w]_B?
questions.explain: The coordinate mapping is linear, so [2u - w]_B = 2[u]_B - [w]_B = (2 - 3, -4 - 1, 0 - 4) = (-1, -5, -4).

questions.q: Let B = {(1, -1), (2, -3)}. The coordinate mapping T(x) = [x]_B can be written as T(x) = Ax. What is A? (Matrices are written row by row.)
questions.explain: Let P = [[1, 2], [-1, -3]], the matrix with the basis vectors as columns. Then x = P[x]_B, so [x]_B = P⁻¹x and A = P⁻¹. det P = -3 + 2 = -1, so P⁻¹ = (1/-1)[[-3, -2], [1, 1]] = [[3, 2], [-1, -1]]. Check: A(1, -1) = (1, 0) and A(2, -3) = (0, 1).

questions.q: For a basis B = {b₁, ..., bₙ} of ℝⁿ, the matrix of the coordinate mapping x ↦ [x]_B is P = [b₁ b₂ ... bₙ], the matrix with the basis vectors as columns.
questions.explain: P takes coordinates to the vector: x = P[x]_B. The coordinate mapping goes the other way, so its matrix is P⁻¹.

questions.q: Let B = {(1, -1), (2, -3)}. The matrix of the coordinate mapping is A = [[3, 2], [-1, -1]]. What is [x]_B for x = (1, 1)?
questions.explain: A(1, 1) = (3 + 2, -1 - 1) = (5, -2). Check: 5(1, -1) - 2(2, -3) = (5 - 4, -5 + 6) = (1, 1). (3, -4) is what the basis matrix P gives, which goes the wrong direction.

questions.q: Let B = {(1, 1), (1, 2)}. What is the matrix A of the coordinate mapping x ↦ [x]_B? (Matrices are written row by row.)
Using the standard basis {1, t, t², t³} of ℙ₃, what is the coordinate vector of p(t) = 3 - t³?
questions.explain: List the coefficients of 1, t, t², t³ in that order, and write a 0 for each missing power: (3, 0, 0, -1).

questions.q: What is the dimension of ℙ₃, the space of polynomials of degree at most 3?
questions.explain: The standard basis {1, t, t², t³} has 4 elements, so dim ℙ₃ = 4 and coordinate vectors for ℙ₃ live in ℝ⁴. In general, dim ℙₙ = n + 1.

questions.q: Using the standard basis {1, t, t², t³}, what is the coordinate vector of p(t) = -2 + t + t² in ℙ₃?
questions.explain: The coefficients of 1, t, t², t³ are -2, 1, 1, 0. Keep the trailing 0 so that the vector is in ℝ⁴.

questions.q: Is {p₁, p₂, p₃, p₄} a basis for ℙ₃, where p₁ = 1 + t + t³, p₂ = t² + 2t³, p₃ = -2 + t + t², and p₄ = 3 - 2t + 2t³?
choices: Yes. The 4×4 matrix of coordinate vectors has a pivot in every column, so the polynomials are independent, and 4 independent vectors in the 4-dimensional space ℙ₃ form a basis.
No. p₂ has no constant term, so the set cannot span ℙ₃.
No. The polynomials are dependent because p₄ = p₁ - p₃.
No. A basis of ℙ₃ must contain exactly 3 polynomials.
questions.explain: The coordinate vectors (1, 1, 0, 1), (0, 0, 1, 2), (-2, 1, 1, 0), (3, -2, 0, 2) row reduce to a matrix with 4 pivots (det = 3). p₁ - p₃ = 3 - t² + t³, which is not p₄. dim ℙ₃ = 4, so a basis has 4 polynomials.

questions.q: Why can you decide whether some polynomials are linearly independent by row reducing a matrix made from their coordinate vectors?
choices: The coordinate mapping is linear and one-to-one, so a combination of the polynomials equals 0 exactly when the same combination of their coordinate vectors equals 0.
Polynomials are literally vectors in ℝⁿ, so no translation is needed.
The coordinate mapping is onto, so any set of coordinate vectors spans ℝⁿ.
Polynomials of different degrees are always linearly independent.
questions.explain: Linearity turns x₁p₁ + ... + xₖpₖ = 0 into x₁[p₁] + ... + xₖ[pₖ] = 0. Because the mapping is one-to-one, the reverse step also works. So both equations have the same solutions.

questions.q: The set {1 + t, t + t², 1 + 2t + t²} is a basis for ℙ₂.
questions.explain: The coordinate vectors are (1, 1, 0), (0, 1, 1), (1, 2, 1). The third is the sum of the first two, since (1 + t) + (t + t²) = 1 + 2t + t². So the set is dependent and is not a basis.

questions.q: B = {1, 1 + t, 1 + t + t²} is a basis for ℙ₂. What is [p]_B for p(t) = 2 + 3t + 4t²?
questions.explain: c₁(1) + c₂(1 + t) + c₃(1 + t + t²) = (c₁ + c₂ + c₃) + (c₂ + c₃)t + c₃t². Matching coefficients: c₃ = 4, c₂ = 3 - 4 = -1, c₁ = 2 - (-1) - 4 = -1. (2, 3, 4) is the coordinate vector for the standard basis, not for B.

questions.q: Which condition defines T : V → W as a linear transformation?
choices: T(u + v) = T(u) + T(v) and T(cv) = cT(v) for all u, v in V and all scalars c.
T(u + v) = T(u) + T(v) for all u, v in V. Scalar multiples do not need to be checked.
T(uv) = T(u)T(v) for all u, v in V.
questions.explain: Both properties (additivity and homogeneity) must hold for all vectors and scalars. T(0) = 0 follows from linearity, but it is not enough to prove it.

questions.q: Which of these maps are linear transformations?
choices: T : ℝ² → ℝ², T(x, y) = (2x - y, 4y)
T : ℝ² → ℝ², T(x, y) = (x², y)
T : ℝ² → ℝ², T(x, y) = (x + y, 1)
T : ℙ₂ → ℙ₂, T(p) = p′ (the derivative)
T : ℙ₂ → ℝ, T(p) = p(2)
T : ℝ² → ℝ², T(x, y) = (|x|, y)
questions.explain: (2x - y, 4y) is a matrix transformation. Differentiation and evaluation respect sums and scalar multiples. (x², y) fails because T(2, 0) = (4, 0) ≠ 2T(1, 0). (x + y, 1) has T(0) = (0, 1) ≠ 0. (|x|, y) fails because T(-1, 0) = (1, 0) ≠ -T(1, 0).

questions.q: If T(0) = 0, then T is a linear transformation.
questions.explain: T(0) = 0 is necessary but not sufficient. For example, T(x, y) = (xy, x) has T(0, 0) = (0, 0), but it is not linear.

questions.q: If T(0) ≠ 0, then T is not a linear transformation.
questions.explain: For any linear T, T(0) = T(0·v) = 0·T(v) = 0. So a map with T(0) ≠ 0 cannot be linear.

questions.q: Which of these shows that T(x, y) = (xy, x) is not linear?
questions.explain: One specific failure of T(cv) = cT(v) is enough to disprove linearity. The other choices are true facts about T, but none of them is a failure of a linearity property.

questions.q: Which statement about checking linearity is correct?
choices: One specific counterexample shows a map is not linear, but proving linearity requires checking both properties for arbitrary u, v and c.
Checking both properties for one particular pair of vectors and one scalar proves a map is linear.
To show a map is not linear, you must show that both properties fail.
A map is linear as soon as it sends the zero vector to the zero vector.
questions.explain: The definition says 'for all u, v and all c'. A proof must be general, while a single failure disproves it. Failing either property is enough.

questions.q: T : ℝ³ → ℝ² is given by T(x, y, z) = (x + 2z, y - z). Which matrix A satisfies T(x) = Ax? (Matrices are written row by row.)
questions.explain: A is 2×3 (m × n for T : ℝⁿ → ℝᵐ). Its columns are T(e₁) = (1, 0), T(e₂) = (0, 1), and T(e₃) = (2, -1).

questions.q: For a linear transformation T : V → W, ker T is a subspace of which space?
choices: V, the domain
W, the codomain
Both V and W
Neither, in general
questions.explain: ker T = {v ∈ V : T(v) = 0} consists of inputs, so it lives in the domain V.

questions.q: For a linear transformation T : V → W, Ran T is a subspace of V.
questions.explain: Ran T = {T(v) : v ∈ V} consists of outputs, so it is a subspace of the codomain W.

questions.q: Which argument shows that ker T is closed under addition?
choices: If u, v ∈ ker T, then T(u + v) = T(u) + T(v) = 0 + 0 = 0, so u + v ∈ ker T.
If u, v ∈ ker T, then u + v = 0, so u + v ∈ ker T.
If u, v ∈ ker T, then T(u + v) = T(u)T(v) = 0, so u + v ∈ ker T.
Since T(0) = 0, every sum of vectors lies in ker T.
questions.explain: Additivity of T gives T(u + v) = T(u) + T(v), and both terms are 0. Closure under scalar multiplication is similar: T(cu) = cT(u) = c0 = 0.

questions.q: T : ℙ₂ → ℝ² is given by T(p) = (p(0), p′(0)). Which set is a basis for ker T?
choices: {t²}
{t, t²}
questions.explain: For p = a₀ + a₁t + a₂t², T(p) = (a₀, a₁). T(p) = 0 forces a₀ = a₁ = 0 with a₂ free, so p = a₂t² and ker T = span{t²}. T(t) = (0, 1) ≠ 0, so t is not in the kernel.

questions.q: T : ℙ₂ → ℝ² is given by T(p) = (p(0), p′(0)). What is Ran T?
choices: All of ℝ²
The line through the origin where both entries are equal
questions.explain: T(a₀ + a₁t + a₂t²) = (a₀, a₁), and a₀, a₁ can be anything. For any (a, b), p(t) = a + bt gives T(p) = (a, b).

questions.q: The map T : ℙ₂ → ℝ², T(p) = (p(0), p′(0)), is one-to-one.
questions.explain: Its kernel span{t²} is nontrivial. For example, T(1 + t) = T(1 + t + t²) = (1, 1).

questions.q: T : ℝ² → ℝ² is given by T(x, y) = (x - y, x + 2y). Which is a basis for ker T?
choices: The empty set ∅ (ker T = {0})
questions.explain: x - y = 0 and x + 2y = 0 give x = y and 3y = 0, so only (0, 0) is in the kernel. The zero subspace has the empty basis. {(0, 0)} is linearly dependent, so it is not a basis.

questions.q: For T : ℝ² → ℝ², T(x, y) = (x - y, x + 2y), the range of T is all of ℝ².
questions.explain: For any (a, b), solving x - y = a and x + 2y = b gives y = (b - a)/3 and x = (2a + b)/3. Equivalently, det [[1, -1], [1, 2]] = 3 ≠ 0.

questions.q: A basis for the zero subspace {0} is {0}.
questions.explain: Any set containing 0 is linearly dependent. The zero subspace has the empty set as its basis and has dimension 0.

questions.q: T : ℝ² → ℝ² is given by T(x, y) = (x - 3y, 2x - 6y). Which is a basis for ker T?
choices: The empty set ∅
questions.explain: Both equations reduce to x = 3y, so (x, y) = y(3, 1). Check: T(3, 1) = (0, 0).

questions.q: T : ℝ² → ℝ² is given by T(x, y) = (x - 3y, 2x - 6y). What is Ran T?
choices: span{(1, 2)}, the line y = 2x
All of ℝ²
questions.explain: T(x, y) = (x - 3y)(1, 2), so every output is a multiple of (1, 2). The range is a line, not all of ℝ². (3, 1) spans the kernel, not the range.

questions.q: T : ℙ₂ → ℝ² is given by T(p) = (p(0), p(2)). Which set is a basis for ker T?
choices: {t² - 2t}
{t²}
questions.explain: For p = a₀ + a₁t + a₂t², p(0) = a₀ = 0 and p(2) = 2a₁ + 4a₂ = 0, so a₁ = -2a₂ and p = a₂(t² - 2t). Check: t² - 2t vanishes at t = 0 and t = 2. t² fails at t = 2, and t² - 2 fails at t = 0.
